intro: You planned sunshine, tacos and boat days — and instead you woke up with a fever, a stuffy nose and aching muscles. Coughs, colds and flu are among the most common reasons travelers call us in Los Cabos, especially during the busy fall and winter season when airports and flights are full and many visitors arrive with something they picked up on the way.

Most colds get better on their own with rest and fluids. The flu and COVID-like illnesses can hit harder, and some people need a doctor quickly. This guide explains how to tell them apart, what helps while you rest, the warning signs not to ignore, and how to see an English-speaking doctor at your hotel, villa or yacht in Cabo San Lucas, the Tourist Corridor or San José del Cabo.

sections.h2: Why travelers get sick in Cabo
p: Getting sick on vacation is rarely about the destination itself. More often it is the trip:
list: Crowded airports and flights where respiratory viruses spread easily.
Less sleep from early flights, late dinners and nights out.
Dehydration from sun, heat and alcohol.
Strong air conditioning that dries out the nose and throat.
Shared spaces — villas, boats and group dinners where one person's cold quickly becomes everyone's.

sections.h2: Cold, flu or COVID-like illness: how they usually differ
p: The symptoms overlap a lot, and only an exam (and sometimes a test) can tell for sure. Still, some patterns are typical:

list: Comes on gradually
Runny or stuffy nose, sneezing and a scratchy throat
Mild cough and tiredness
Fever is uncommon or low
Starts suddenly — many people can name the hour it hit
Fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills and sweats
Body aches, headache and strong fatigue
Dry cough; sometimes vomiting or diarrhea, especially in children
Can look like either a cold or the flu
Fever, cough, sore throat, congestion and fatigue
New loss of taste or smell can occur
Shortness of breath in some people

p_after: Because these illnesses look so similar, it is best not to self-diagnose or start leftover prescriptions from home. A doctor can examine you, check your breathing, discuss whether testing makes sense and recommend the right treatment for you.

p: These general steps can make you more comfortable. They do not replace medical care:
list: Rest. Skip the excursion or the beach club for a day or two — your body recovers faster.
Drink plenty of fluids: bottled or purified water, broth, warm tea or electrolyte drinks.
Stay out of the midday sun and avoid alcohol while you have a fever.
Ease congestion with a steamy shower and by setting the air conditioning a little warmer at night.
Eat light, simple meals when you feel up to it.

Ask before taking medicine. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using fever reducers, cough or cold products, especially for children, during pregnancy, or if you take other medication or have health conditions. Brand names and ingredients in Mexico can differ from those at home.
Protect your travel group: wash hands often, cover coughs, avoid sharing cups and consider keeping some distance from older or vulnerable family members.

sections.h2: When to see a doctor — and when to call 911
p: Arrange a doctor visit the same day if you have:
list: A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher that lasts more than a day or two, or keeps coming back
A cough that is getting worse, or symptoms that improve and then suddenly get worse again
Ear pain, sinus pain or a very sore throat along with fever
Trouble keeping fluids down, little or no urination, or dizziness when standing
Symptoms in a baby or young child, an adult over 65, someone pregnant, or anyone with asthma, diabetes, heart or lung disease or a weakened immune system
A long flight home coming up and you want to know whether you are fit to travel
p_after: Call 911 right away if you or someone with you has trouble breathing or shortness of breath at rest, chest pain or pressure, bluish lips or face, confusion or difficulty waking up, a seizure, severe weakness, or a high fever with a stiff neck or a rash. In children, also call for very fast breathing, ribs pulling in with each breath, no tears when crying or no wet diapers for many hours. These can be signs of a serious illness that needs emergency care.

sections.h2: Seeing a doctor in Cabo without leaving your room

p: When you have a fever and aches, the last thing you want is a taxi ride and a waiting room. An English-speaking doctor comes to your hotel, villa or yacht 24/7, listens to your lungs, checks your throat, ears and vital signs, and prescribes treatment if appropriate. Typical arrival is 30–45 minutes in Cabo San Lucas and the Tourist Corridor, and up to about 60 minutes in San José del Cabo, Pedregal and Palmilla. Book a house-call doctor.
Feeling well enough to go out and staying near downtown? You can be seen at our clinic on Francisco I. Madero, Centro, Cabo San Lucas, for $99 USD.
Prescriptions, tissues, a thermometer, bottled water and electrolyte drinks can be delivered to your room 24/7 — free over $50 USD (a fee may apply between 10 PM and 7 AM). Order pharmacy delivery.

p_after: There is no payment before the visit, and you receive an itemized invoice in English and USD for your travel insurance (US and Canadian insurance accepted, subject to verification). See every rate on our prices page.

p: Fever, sweating and a poor appetite can leave you dehydrated. Some travelers choose an IV drip for fluid and wellness support once a doctor confirms it is appropriate for them. Options include Immunity Armor ($159 at your door) or Rapid Hydration ($159). An IV drip is not a treatment or cure for the flu, COVID or any infection, and it does not replace a medical evaluation when you are sick.
p_after: If several people in your villa are run down, the doctor can see everyone during the same visit, and groups of 6 or more can book group IV therapy at $119 USD per person, tax included.

sections.h2: Tips to stay healthy for the rest of your trip
list: Get a full night's sleep after your travel day.
Carry a refillable bottle of purified water and sip through the day.
Alternate alcoholic drinks with water, especially in the sun.
Wash hands before meals and after airports, taxis and boats.
If one person in your group gets sick, give them their own towels and cups.
Pack a small kit with a thermometer and the medications you normally use at home.

faq.q: Can a doctor come to my hotel in Cabo if I have the flu?
faq.a: Yes. Our English-speaking doctors make house calls to hotels, villas and yachts 24/7 for $189 USD. Typical arrival is 30 to 45 minutes in Cabo San Lucas and the Tourist Corridor, and up to about 60 minutes in San José del Cabo, Pedregal and Palmilla.

faq.q: How do I know if it is a cold, the flu or COVID?
faq.a: Colds usually start slowly with a runny nose and little or no fever, while the flu tends to hit suddenly with fever and body aches. COVID-like illness can look like either. Only an exam and sometimes testing can tell for sure, so a doctor visit is the best way to know.

faq.q: Can I buy cold and flu medicine at a pharmacy in Cabo?
faq.a: Many over-the-counter products are available, but brand names and ingredients can differ from home, and antibiotics and antivirals require a prescription in Mexico. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything, especially for children or if you take other medication.

faq.q: Will my travel insurance cover a doctor visit for the flu?
faq.a: Many travel insurance plans reimburse doctor visits abroad. You pay after the visit and receive an itemized invoice in English and USD to submit to your insurer. We accept international health and travel insurance from the United States and Canada, subject to policy verification and coverage confirmation.

faq.q: When are flu symptoms an emergency?
faq.a: Call 911 for trouble breathing, chest pain or pressure, bluish lips, confusion or difficulty waking, a seizure, severe weakness, or a high fever with a stiff neck or rash.
